teaser: A Deposition from the Cross with no cross, no ground and no shadows. Only pink and blue.
review_notes:
Capponi Chapel, Santa Felicita, Florence: chapel built by Brunelleschi for the Barbadori, bought by Lodovico Capponi in 1525; altarpiece c. 1525-28, about 313 x 192 cm, on wood, still in its original frame and place.
Vasari: Pontormo kept the chapel closed with screens for three years; Vasari disliked the result's lack of shadow.
Bearded man at right edge traditionally identified as a self-portrait.
Bronzino, his pupil, assisted in the chapel (roundels of the Evangelists).
Palette linked to Michelangelo's Sistine ceiling; cleaning/restoration completed 2017-18.
Pontormo's diary (1554-56) recording meals and health.
Subject debated: Deposition, Entombment or a Lamentation; lesson says so.

lesson.text: Count the crosses in this Deposition from the Cross. Then count the ladders, the nails, the hills, the tombs. The total is zero. Eleven people fill the panel, and behind them there is only a gray-blue haze and one small cloud.

Jacopo Carucci, called Pontormo after his home village, painted it between about 1525 and 1528 for a banker's burial chapel in Santa Felicita, a small church a few steps from the Ponte Vecchio in Florence. It has never left. You still see it in the chapel it was made for, in its original gilded frame.

A “deposition” is the moment when Christ's body is taken down from the cross. Painters before Pontormo loved its machinery: beams, ropes, men on ladders. He removed all of it and kept only the people and their shock. So what holds the picture up?
With no architecture and no landscape, the bodies themselves have to be the structure.

lines.label: A wheel of faces
lines.text: Join the heads and you get a loop turning around the middle of the panel. Your eye circles from face to face and never finds a place to rest.

lines.label: The body
lines.text: Christ's pale body sags in a long curve from his head to his feet. It is the heaviest thing in the picture, carried by its two lightest figures.

lines.label: Mother and son
lines.text: A slanting line links Mary's face to her son's. She is tipping backward, he is being carried forward. The distance between them is growing as you watch.

lesson.text: That is the real subject: a separation. Some scholars think the body is not coming down from a cross at all but being carried away from its mother toward the tomb. Pontormo leaves the story open and paints the instant her hands lose him.

According to the biographer Giorgio Vasari, Pontormo boarded up the chapel with screens and worked behind them for three years. Not even the patron who was paying was allowed to peek until the day it was unveiled.

When Florence finally saw it, the color was the shock. Candy pink, sky blue, a green like unripe apples, with hardly a shadow anywhere. Vasari complained that it had no darkness in it. The chapel is dim, and these pale tones were chosen to glow in poor light.

The colors had a source. Pontormo admired Michelangelo, who had painted the prophets on the Sistine Chapel ceiling in the same sharp, shifting hues: cloth that is pink in the light and blue in the fold. Pontormo took that trick and made it the mood of an entire picture.

lesson.title: Weightless
lesson.text: The scene shows people carrying a dead man. Check how much effort it seems to cost them.

spots.title: The crouching bearer
spots.text: He takes the whole torso on his shoulder, yet his face shows no strain, only wide wet eyes turned to you. His clothes are a second skin of pink and blue.

spots.title: Tiptoes
spots.text: He balances on the balls of his feet, toes barely touching a patch of green. Nobody could carry a grown man like this. The weight is emotional, not physical.

spots.title: The empty middle
spots.text: At the center of the panel there is no face at all: only a knot of hands, a white cloth and the dead man's limp fingers. The heart of the picture is a gap.

spots.title: The cloud
spots.text: One solid little cloud, the only piece of the outside world. It tells you there is air around these people, and nothing else.

lesson.text: Did you feel how the figures float? There is almost no ground, no cast shadow to pin anyone down, and the people at the top seem stacked rather than standing behind. Pontormo gave up the calm, measurable space that Renaissance painters had spent a century perfecting.
Pontormo strips a sacred story of its setting so that only feeling remains. Color and gesture do the work that scenery used to do.

This restless style, later labeled Mannerism, grew in an anxious decade. Rome was sacked by imperial troops in 1527, and plague and siege came to Florence while Pontormo was at work or soon after. His wide-eyed mourners look like people who no longer trust the ground.
One person stands apart from the grief, at the edge, looking out at you. He is thought to be the painter. Where is he?

spots.title: Pontormo himself
spots.text: A bearded man in a green cap and ocher cloak is squeezed against the right edge. Tradition says it is a self-portrait: the artist as a witness, half inside his own vision.

lesson.text: He was in his early thirties, already known as solitary and hard to deal with. Vasari says he lived in a house whose upper room could only be reached by a ladder, which he pulled up behind him when he wanted to be left alone.
In his last years Pontormo kept a diary. It says almost nothing about art. It lists what he ate each day, an egg, some bread, a little lamb, along with notes on his stomach and the weather.

For centuries the picture was seen as an oddity. In the 1900s, painters and filmmakers rediscovered it and found its acid colors strangely modern. A recent cleaning removed layers of grime, and the pinks came back even louder than anyone expected.

The chapel was designed a century earlier by Filippo Brunelleschi, the architect of Florence's cathedral dome. Pontormo decorated it with the help of a teenage pupil named Bronzino, who would become the favorite portraitist of the Medici court.

quiz.question: What is missing from this Deposition from the Cross?
quiz.explanation: There is no cross, ladder or tomb, only figures against a hazy sky.

quiz.question: Where can you see the painting today?
options: In the chapel in Santa Felicita, Florence, that it was made for
quiz.explanation: It has never left its chapel and still sits in its original frame.

quiz.question: Whose colors inspired Pontormo's pinks and blues?
quiz.explanation: He borrowed the sharp, shifting hues of Michelangelo's Sistine prophets.

quiz.question: What sits at the very center of the panel?
options: A knot of hands and a white cloth
quiz.explanation: The middle is an empty zone of hands, with the faces turning around it.

quiz.question: What did Pontormo record in his late diary?
options: Mostly what he ate each day
quiz.explanation: The diary lists meals, health and weather, and says very little about art.

facts.text: Pontormo let the patron watch him paint the chapel day by day.
facts.explanation: Vasari says he screened it off for three years and let no one in.

facts.text: The bearded man at the right edge is traditionally seen as a self-portrait.
facts.explanation: Tradition identifies the man in the green cap as Pontormo himself.

facts.text: The figures cast strong, dark shadows on the ground.
facts.explanation: There is almost no ground or shadow, which is why they seem to float.
